items.stem: Which is the definition of the moment of a force about a point?
options: Force × perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force
Force × distance from the point to where the force acts, in any direction
Force × distance moved by the force
items.answer: Force × perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force
items.markingKey: Moment = F × d⊥.

items.stem: Explain why it is easier to undo a tight nut with a long spanner.
items.answer: The moment is F × perpendicular distance; a longer spanner gives a larger distance so the same moment needs a smaller force.
items.markingKey: moment = F × d [1]; larger d, smaller F for same moment [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a couple causes rotation but no acceleration of the centre of mass.
items.answer: The two forces are equal and opposite so the resultant force is zero (no translation), but their moments add, giving a resultant torque.
items.markingKey: resultant force zero [1]; moments in same sense give torque [1] [2]

items.stem: A cyclist presses on a pedal crank of length 0.60 m with a force of 25 N, perpendicular to it. Calculate the moment of the force about the pivot.
items.answer: 15 N m
items.markingKey: M = F × d⊥ = 25 × 0.60 = 15 N m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Isla pushes on a door 0.30 m from its hinge with a force of 80 N at 60° to it. Calculate the moment produced. The nut needs a moment of 15 N m to turn. Calculate the minimum force needed at the same point, and explain why it is a minimum.
items.answer: 20.8 N m; 50 N applied perpendicular to the spanner (largest perpendicular distance)
items.markingKey: M = F d sin θ = 20.8 N m [1]; F = 15/0.30 [1]; = 50 N [1]; perpendicular force gives maximum moment arm [1] [4]

items.stem: A plumber turns a valve wheel of radius 0.15 m by pushing and pulling with forces of 25 N tangentially at opposite ends of a diameter. (a) Calculate the torque of the couple. (b) State the resultant force on the brace and explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) 7.5 N m (b) Zero: the forces are equal and opposite.
items.markingKey: (a) 25 × 0.30 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 7.5 N m with unit [1] [2] (b) zero [1]; equal and opposite [1] [2]

items.stem: What is a couple?
options: Two equal forces in the same direction
Two forces that are Newton's third law pairs
A pair of equal and opposite forces whose lines of action do not coincide
A single force acting through the pivot
items.answer: A pair of equal and opposite forces whose lines of action do not coincide
items.markingKey: A couple produces rotation without translation.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which is the definition of the moment of a force about a point? (b) What is the SI unit of moment of a force?
items.answer: (a) Force × perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force (b) N m
items.markingKey: (a) Moment = F × d⊥. (b) Force (N) × distance (m).

items.stem: Explain why a door handle is placed far from the hinges.
items.answer: The perpendicular distance from the hinge (pivot) is large, so a small force produces a large enough moment to turn the door.
items.markingKey: large perpendicular distance from pivot [1]; small force needed [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why pushing a door at an angle to its surface is less effective than pushing perpendicularly.
items.answer: Only the component of force perpendicular to the door (F sin θ) produces a moment; the perpendicular distance from the hinge to the line of action is smaller.
items.markingKey: only perpendicular component turns [1]; smaller moment for same force [1] [2]

items.stem: Show that the torque of a couple is the same about any point.
items.answer: Take a point a distance x from one force, separation d: moments are F(x + d) and −Fx; total = Fd, independent of x.
items.markingKey: moments about arbitrary point [1]; x cancels leaving Fd [1] [2]

items.stem: A tap is turned by forces of 15 N applied in opposite directions at the ends of a handle 0.80 m long, perpendicular to it. Calculate the torque of the couple.
items.answer: 12 N m
items.markingKey: torque = F × perpendicular separation = 15 × 0.80 [1]; = 12 N m [1] [2]

items.stem: Ethan pushes on a door 0.40 m from its hinge with a force of 50 N at 70° to it. Determine the moment of the force about the pivot.
items.markingKey: M = F × d⊥ = 50 × 0.40 × sin 70° = 18.8 N m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A driver turns a steering wheel of diameter 0.24 m by applying equal and opposite forces of 20 N tangentially at opposite ends of a diameter. Calculate the torque of the couple.
items.answer: 4.8 N m
items.markingKey: torque = F × perpendicular separation = 20 × 0.24 [1]; = 4.8 N m [1] [2]

items.stem: A cyclist presses on a pedal crank of length 0.80 m with a force of 80 N at 60° to it. Calculate the moment produced. The nut needs a moment of 15 N m to turn. Calculate the minimum force needed at the same point, and explain why it is a minimum.
items.answer: 55.4 N m; 18.8 N applied perpendicular to the spanner (largest perpendicular distance)
items.markingKey: M = F d sin θ = 55.4 N m [1]; F = 15/0.80 [1]; = 18.8 N [1]; perpendicular force gives maximum moment arm [1] [4]

items.stem: A mechanic in Kuala Lumpur uses a two-handed wheel brace with arms of length 0.20 m each side of the nut. She applies forces of 20 N perpendicular to the arms at each end, in opposite directions. (a) A single force of 20 N is instead applied at one end at 50° to the arm (or radius). Calculate its moment about the centre. (b) Define the moment of a force.
items.answer: (a) 3.06 N m (b) Force × perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force.
items.markingKey: (a) F d sin θ (method/substitution) [1]; answer 3.06 N m with unit [1] [2] (b) Force × perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force [1]

items.stem: A mechanic in Doha uses a two-handed wheel brace with arms of length 0.15 m each side of the nut. She applies forces of 40 N perpendicular to the arms at each end, in opposite directions. (a) Calculate the torque of the couple. (b) Explain why the moment arm is measured perpendicular to the line of action.
items.answer: (a) 12 N m (b) Only the perpendicular distance determines the turning effect; a component along the arm passes through the pivot and has no moment.
items.markingKey: (a) 40 × 0.30 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 12 N m with unit [1] [2] (b) perpendicular distance determines turning [1]; component through pivot gives no moment [1] [2]

items.stem: A plumber turns a valve wheel of radius 0.30 m by pushing and pulling with forces of 20 N tangentially at opposite ends of a diameter. (a) A single force of 20 N is instead applied at one end at 70° to the arm (or radius). Calculate its moment about the centre. (b) Define the moment of a force. (c) Explain why the moment arm is measured perpendicular to the line of action.
items.answer: (a) 5.64 N m (b) Force × perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force. (c) Only the perpendicular distance determines the turning effect; a component along the arm passes through the pivot and has no moment.
items.markingKey: (a) F d sin θ (method/substitution) [1]; answer 5.64 N m with unit [1] [2] (b) Force × perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force [1] (c) perpendicular distance determines turning [1]; component through pivot gives no moment [1] [2]

items.stem: State the two conditions for an object to be in equilibrium.
items.answer: There is no resultant force and no resultant moment (torque) about any point.
items.markingKey: resultant force zero [1]; resultant moment zero [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a ladder leaning against a smooth wall needs friction at the ground to stay in equilibrium.
items.answer: The smooth wall gives only a horizontal normal force; for zero resultant horizontal force, an equal and opposite horizontal force (friction at the ground) is needed.
items.markingKey: wall force horizontal [1]; friction balances it [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why taking moments about the point where an unknown force acts simplifies a problem.
items.answer: That force has zero moment about its own point of application, so it does not appear in the equation and another unknown can be found.
items.markingKey: zero moment about its own point [1]; eliminates unknown [1] [2]

items.stem: A uniform shelf of length 3.0 m and weight 400 N rests on brackets at its ends A and B. A box of weight 600 N is 0.75 m from A. Calculate the force exerted by support B.
items.markingKey: moments about A: R_B × 3.0 = 400 × 1.5 + 600 × 0.75 = 350 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A uniform plank of length 3.0 m and weight 100 N rests on supports at its ends A and B. A load of 600 N is placed 0.90 m from A. Calculate the forces exerted by both supports.
items.markingKey: moments about A [1]; R_B = 230 N [1]; R_A = 700 − R_B = 470 N [1] [3]

items.stem: A uniform plank of length 2.0 m and weight 400 N rests on supports at its ends A and B. A load of 200 N is placed 1.5 m from A. (a) Calculate the force from each support. (b) Determine how far from A the load must be for the force at B to equal the force at A. (c) State the two conditions for equilibrium used.
items.answer: (a) A 250 N, B 350 N (b) 1.0 m (the centre) (c) zero resultant force and zero resultant moment.
items.markingKey: (a) moments about A [1]; R_B = 350 N [1]; R_A = 250 N [1] (b) equal forces require load at centre by symmetry [1] (c) both conditions [1] [5]

items.stem: A uniform diving board of length 4.0 m and weight 300 N is supported at both ends A and B. (a) State the principle of moments. (b) Calculate the force at A. (c) Explain why the weight of a uniform board can be taken to act at its midpoint.
items.answer: (a) In equilibrium, sum of clockwise moments = sum of anticlockwise moments about any point. (b) 300 N (c) For a uniform board the centre of gravity is at its geometric centre.
items.markingKey: (a) clockwise moments = anticlockwise moments [1]; about the same point, body in equilibrium [1] [2] (b) vertical equilibrium: 300 N [1] (c) For a uniform board the centre of gravity is at its geometric centre [1]

items.stem: A uniform diving board of length 6.0 m and weight 500 N is supported at both ends A and B. (a) State the principle of moments. (b) A person of weight 600 N stands 4.5 m from A. Calculate the force at B. (c) Explain why the weight of a uniform board can be taken to act at its midpoint.
items.answer: (a) In equilibrium, sum of clockwise moments = sum of anticlockwise moments about any point. (b) 700 N (c) For a uniform board the centre of gravity is at its geometric centre.
items.markingKey: (a) clockwise moments = anticlockwise moments [1]; about the same point, body in equilibrium [1] [2] (b) moments about A (method/substitution) [1]; answer 700 N with unit [1] [2] (c) For a uniform board the centre of gravity is at its geometric centre [1]

items.stem: State the principle of moments.
items.answer: For a body in equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about the same point.
items.markingKey: clockwise = anticlockwise [1]; about the same point, in equilibrium [1] [2]

items.stem: Three forces act on a body in equilibrium. When drawn tip to tail, the vectors form …
options: a right angle in every case
items.answer: a closed triangle
items.markingKey: Zero resultant: the vector triangle closes.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Three forces acting on a body in equilibrium must … (b) Three forces act on a body in equilibrium. When drawn tip to tail, the vectors form …
items.answer: (a) pass through a single point (if not parallel) (b) a closed triangle
items.markingKey: (a) Otherwise they would produce a resultant moment. (b) Zero resultant: the vector triangle closes.

items.stem: Describe how a triangle of forces is used to find an unknown force on an object in equilibrium.
items.answer: Draw the known forces to scale tip to tail in their directions; the line that closes the triangle gives the magnitude and direction of the unknown force.
items.markingKey: scale drawing tip to tail [1]; closing side gives the unknown [1] [2]

items.stem: A picture hangs from a nail by a string with its two halves at equal angles to the horizontal. Explain why the tension increases as the string is made more nearly horizontal.
items.answer: The vertical components 2T sin θ must equal the weight; as θ decreases, sin θ decreases, so T must increase.
items.markingKey: 2T sin θ = W [1]; smaller θ needs larger T [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why a ladder leaning against a smooth wall needs friction at the ground to stay in equilibrium. (b) Describe how a triangle of forces is used to find an unknown force on an object in equilibrium.

(b) Draw the known forces to scale tip to tail in their directions; the line that closes the triangle gives the magnitude and direction of the unknown force.
items.markingKey: (a) wall force horizontal [1]; friction balances it [1] [2] (b) scale drawing tip to tail [1]; closing side gives the unknown [1] [2]

items.stem: A uniform shelf of length 2.0 m and weight 200 N rests on brackets at its ends A and B. A box of weight 800 N is 0.60 m from A. What is the force exerted by support B?
A uniform plank of length 2.0 m and weight 300 N rests on supports at its ends A and B. A load of 600 N is placed 0.40 m from A. What is the force exerted by support B?

A ball of weight 30 N hangs on a string. A horizontal force F pulls the ball sideways so that the string makes 60° with the vertical, and the ball is in equilibrium. By drawing a triangle of forces or resolving, determine F and the tension in the string.
items.markingKey: vertical: T cos 60° = 30 [1]; T = 60.0 N [1]; horizontal: F = T sin 60° [1]; = 52.0 N [1] [4]

items.stem: A uniform bridge of length 5.0 m and weight 200 N is supported at each end. A person of weight 400 N stands 1.25 m from end A. Calculate the force exerted by support B.
items.markingKey: moments about A: R_B × 5.0 = 200 × 2.5 + 400 × 1.25 = 200 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A sign of weight 20 N is suspended from the middle of a cable whose two halves are each at 60° to the horizontal. Calculate the tension in the wire.
items.markingKey: vertical equilibrium: 2T sin 60° = 20 [1]; T = 20/(2 sin 60°) [1]; = 11.5 N [1] [3]

items.stem: A uniform horizontal beam of length 1.5 m and weight 60 N is hinged to a wall at one end. A sign of weight 50 N hangs from the other end, which is held by a cable at 40° above the horizontal attached to the wall. Calculate the tension in the cable and the horizontal and vertical components of the force at the hinge.
items.answer: T = 124 N; hinge: horizontal 95.3 N, vertical 30 N upwards
items.markingKey: moments about hinge: T sin 40° × 1.5 = 60 × 0.75 + 50 × 1.5 [1]; T = 124 N [1]; horizontal: H = T cos 40° = 95.3 N [1]; vertical: V = 110 − T sin 40° = 30 N [1] [4]

items.stem: A uniform gangplank of length 6.0 m and weight 400 N rests on a support at each end, A and B, at a port in Kuala Lumpur. (a) State the principle of moments. (b) A person of weight 700 N stands 4.5 m from A. Calculate the force at B.
items.answer: (a) In equilibrium, sum of clockwise moments = sum of anticlockwise moments about any point. (b) 725 N
items.markingKey: (a) clockwise moments = anticlockwise moments [1]; about the same point, body in equilibrium [1] [2] (b) moments about A (method/substitution) [1]; answer 725 N with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: A uniform diving board of length 5.0 m and weight 300 N is supported at both ends A and B. (a) A person of weight 800 N stands 3.75 m from A. Calculate the force at B. (b) Explain how the force at A changes as the person walks towards B. (c) Explain why the weight of a uniform board can be taken to act at its midpoint.
items.answer: (a) 750 N (b) It decreases, because the moment of the person's weight about B decreases. (c) For a uniform board the centre of gravity is at its geometric centre.
items.markingKey: (a) moments about A (method/substitution) [1]; answer 750 N with unit [1] [2] (b) decreases [1]; reason using moments [1] [2] (c) For a uniform board the centre of gravity is at its geometric centre [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the centre of gravity of an object?
options: The lowest point of the object
The geometric centre of every object
The point through which the whole weight of the object may be considered to act
The point where the mass is greatest
items.answer: The point through which the whole weight of the object may be considered to act
items.markingKey: Definition of centre of gravity.

items.stem: Describe how to find the centre of gravity of an irregular piece of card.
items.answer: Hang it freely from a pin through one hole with a plumb line; draw the vertical line; repeat from another hole; the centre of gravity is where the lines cross.
items.markingKey: suspend freely with plumb line [1]; mark vertical [1]; repeat and intersect [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why racing cars are designed to be low and wide.
items.answer: A low centre of gravity and a wide base mean the car must tilt through a large angle before its weight acts outside the base, so it is less likely to topple on bends.
items.markingKey: low c.g. [1]; wide base [1]; larger tilt needed to topple [1] [3]

items.stem: A fridge (treated as a uniform block) has a base width of 0.40 m and a height of 1.0 m. It is tilted about one edge of its base. Calculate the angle of tilt from the vertical at which it just topples (in degrees).
items.markingKey: tan θ = (w/2)/(h/2) = 0.40/1.0 = 21.8°. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A uniform rectangular cabinet has a base width of 0.60 m and a height of 2.0 m. It is tilted about one edge of its base. Its weight is 300 N. (a) Calculate the angle of tilt at which it topples. (b) Calculate the minimum horizontal force applied at the top edge needed to start tipping it, assuming it does not slide.
items.markingKey: (a) tan θ = 0.60/2.0 [1]; θ = 16.7° [1] (b) moments about the tipping edge: F × 2.0 = 300 × 0.30 [1]; F = 45 N [1] [4]

items.stem: A loaded lorry has its wheels 1.8 m apart and its centre of gravity 1.0 m above the road, midway between the wheels. (a) Explain why loading passengers on the upper deck reduces the angle of tilt at which it topples. (b) Suggest two design features that increase stability.
items.answer: (a) The centre of gravity rises, so a smaller tilt moves the line of action of the weight outside the wheelbase. (b) Wider wheelbase; heavy components (engine, fuel tank) mounted low.
items.markingKey: (a) c.g. higher [1]; smaller tilt needed [1] [2] (b) wider base [1]; lower centre of gravity / heavy parts low [1] [2]

items.stem: Which change makes a bus more stable?
options: Carrying heavy luggage on the roof
items.answer: Lowering its centre of gravity
items.markingKey: A lower centre of gravity and wider base increase stability.

items.stem: Explain why a person carrying a heavy bag in one hand leans the other way.
items.answer: Leaning moves the combined centre of gravity back over the feet (the base) so there is no resultant moment that would cause toppling.
items.markingKey: combined c.g. moves [1]; kept above base [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a tall, thin vase is easily knocked over.
items.answer: Its centre of gravity is high and its base narrow, so only a small tilt moves the line of action of the weight outside the base, giving a toppling moment.
items.markingKey: high c.g. and narrow base [1]; small tilt makes weight act outside base [1] [2]

items.stem: A tapered wooden beam of length 1.5 m rests horizontally on two bathroom scales, one at each end, A and B. Scale A reads 41.6 N and scale B reads 78.4 N. Determine the weight and the distance of the centre of gravity from A.
items.answer: W = 120 N; 0.98 m from A
items.markingKey: W = sum of readings = 120 N [1]; moments about A: 120 × x = 78.4 × 1.5 [1]; x = 0.98 m [1] [3]

items.stem: A uniform bookcase has a base width of 0.40 m and a height of 0.80 m. It is tilted about one edge of its base. Calculate the angle of tilt from the vertical at which it just topples (in degrees).
items.markingKey: tan θ = (w/2)/(h/2) = 0.40/0.80 = 26.6°. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A non-uniform pole of length 2.0 m rests horizontally on two bathroom scales, one at each end, A and B. Scale A reads 14 N and scale B reads 26 N. Determine the weight and the distance of the centre of gravity from A.
items.answer: W = 40 N; 1.3 m from A
items.markingKey: W = sum of readings = 40 N [1]; moments about A: 40 × x = 26 × 2.0 [1]; x = 1.3 m [1] [3]

items.stem: A uniform block has a base width of 0.50 m and a height of 2.4 m. It is tilted about one edge of its base. Its weight is 800 N. (a) Calculate the angle of tilt at which it topples. items.stem: A tap is turned by forces of 12 N applied in opposite directions at the ends of a handle 0.80 m long, perpendicular to it. items.stem: A uniform metre rule is balanced at its 50 cm mark. A 2.0 N weight hangs at the 20 cm mark. Where must a 3.0 N weight hang to balance it?
items.answer: At the 70 cm mark

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Describe how a triangle of forces is used to find an unknown force on an object in equilibrium. (b) A picture hangs from a nail by a string with its two halves at equal angles to the horizontal. Explain why the tension increases as the string is made more nearly horizontal.
items.answer: (a) Draw the known forces to scale tip to tail in their directions; the line that closes the triangle gives the magnitude and direction of the unknown force. (b) The vertical components 2T sin θ must equal the weight; as θ decreases, sin θ decreases, so T must increase.
items.markingKey: (a) scale drawing tip to tail [1]; closing side gives the unknown [1] [2] (b) 2T sin θ = W [1]; smaller θ needs larger T [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why a ladder leaning against a smooth wall needs friction at the ground to stay in equilibrium. (b) Describe how a triangle of forces is used to find an unknown force on an object in equilibrium.
items.answer: (a) The smooth wall gives only a horizontal normal force; for zero resultant horizontal force, an equal and opposite horizontal force (friction at the ground) is needed. (b) Draw the known forces to scale tip to tail in their directions; the line that closes the triangle gives the magnitude and direction of the unknown force.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why a tall, thin vase is easily knocked over. (b) Explain why racing cars are designed to be low and wide.
items.answer: (a) Its centre of gravity is high and its base narrow, so only a small tilt moves the line of action of the weight outside the base, giving a toppling moment. (b) A low centre of gravity and a wide base mean the car must tilt through a large angle before its weight acts outside the base, so it is less likely to topple on bends.
items.markingKey: (a) high c.g. and narrow base [1]; small tilt makes weight act outside base [1] [2] (b) low c.g. [1]; wide base [1]; larger tilt needed to topple [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why a person carrying a heavy bag in one hand leans the other way. (b) Explain why racing cars are designed to be low and wide.
items.answer: (a) Leaning moves the combined centre of gravity back over the feet (the base) so there is no resultant moment that would cause toppling. (b) A low centre of gravity and a wide base mean the car must tilt through a large angle before its weight acts outside the base, so it is less likely to topple on bends.
items.markingKey: (a) combined c.g. moves [1]; kept above base [1] [2] (b) low c.g. [1]; wide base [1]; larger tilt needed to topple [1] [3]

items.stem: What is the SI unit of moment of a force?
items.answer: N m

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why pushing a door at an angle to its surface is less effective than pushing perpendicularly. (b) Show that the torque of a couple is the same about any point.
items.answer: (a) Only the component of force perpendicular to the door (F sin θ) produces a moment; the perpendicular distance from the hinge to the line of action is smaller. (b) Take a point a distance x from one force, separation d: moments are F(x + d) and −Fx; total = Fd, independent of x.
items.markingKey: (a) only perpendicular component turns [1]; smaller moment for same force [1] [2] (b) moments about arbitrary point [1]; x cancels leaving Fd [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why pushing a door at an angle to its surface is less effective than pushing perpendicularly. (b) Explain why it is easier to undo a tight nut with a long spanner.
items.answer: (a) Only the component of force perpendicular to the door (F sin θ) produces a moment; the perpendicular distance from the hinge to the line of action is smaller. (b) The moment is F × perpendicular distance; a longer spanner gives a larger distance so the same moment needs a smaller force.
items.markingKey: (a) only perpendicular component turns [1]; smaller moment for same force [1] [2] (b) moment = F × d [1]; larger d, smaller F for same moment [1] [2]
